# Related work — 20 recent papers (2024–2026)

Compiled 2026-09-20 for *"Towards Autonomous Industrial Mobility: An AI Framework for Optimal
Path Planning and Resource-Efficient Navigation"*.

Every entry was verified against the arXiv API or Crossref on the compile date: title, authors,
year and identifier are taken from the publisher's metadata, not from memory. Each paper is
mapped to the part of this thesis it supports.

---

## A. Neuro-symbolic decision making — the core contribution (WP5/WP6/WP9)

### 1. BANSAI: Towards Bridging the AI Adoption Gap in Industrial Robotics with Neurosymbolic Programming
Benjamin Alt, Julia Dvorak, Darko Katic, Rainer Jäkel, Michael Beetz, Gisela Lanza — arXiv:2404.13652 (21 Apr 2024)
https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.13652
*Why it matters here:* the closest published statement of this thesis's premise — that industrial
robotics adopts AI only when learned components sit inside a symbolic, inspectable program. Cite
it in the introduction as the motivation for a hybrid rather than an end-to-end policy.

### 2. Neuro-Symbolic Reinforcement Learning for Context-Aware Decision Making in Safe Autonomous Vehicles
Huma Khan, Tarunika D. Chaudhari, J. V. N. Ramesh, A. Smitha Kranthi, E. Muniyandy, Y. A. B. El-Ebiary,
D. N. P. Devadhas — IJACSA 16(5), 2025. DOI 10.14569/IJACSA.2025.0160558
https://doi.org/10.14569/IJACSA.2025.0160558
*Why:* same architecture pattern as ours — a symbolic layer enforcing hard rules, a neural layer
ranking within what the rules allow, and an explanation for every decision. Different domain
(driving), so it is a comparison point, not a competitor.

### 3. Supporting Human-Robot Collaboration and Safety with the Proposed Explainable Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning
Rafał Kozik, Aleksandra Pawlicka, Marek Pawlicki et al. — LNCS, *Availability, Reliability and Security*, 2025.
DOI 10.1007/978-3-032-00642-4_15
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-00642-4_15
*Why:* argues explicitly that safety in industrial robotics needs symbolic reasoning to be
auditable. Supports our WP9 finding that only the rule-carrying policies were safe by construction.

### 4. CausalTrace: A Neurosymbolic Causal Analysis Agent for Smart Manufacturing
Chathurangi Shyalika, Aryaman Sharma, Fadi El Kalach et al. — arXiv:2510.12033 (14 Oct 2025)
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.12033
*Why:* neurosymbolic reasoning over factory state, with interpretability as the stated goal.
Useful for positioning our symbolic layer as part of a wider 2025 trend in manufacturing AI.

---

## B. Safe learning, action masking and shielding — the PPO comparison and the ±1 bound (WP6/WP9)

### 5. Integrating Human Knowledge Through Action Masking in Reinforcement Learning for Operations Research
Mirko Stappert, Bernhard Lutz, Niklas Goby, Dirk Neumann — arXiv:2504.02662 (3 Apr 2025)
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.02662
*Why:* the direct reference for our MaskablePPO baseline and for the `ppo_unmasked` ablation.
It formalises masking as injecting human knowledge — exactly the question our ablation answers
empirically (without the mask, PPO scores 28.2 and is unsafe in 11.7 % of shifts).

### 6. Realizable Continuous-Space Shields for Safe Reinforcement Learning
Kyungmin Kim, Davide Corsi, Andoni Rodriguez et al. — arXiv:2410.02038 (2 Oct 2024)
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.02038
*Why:* shielding = a correctness layer that filters a learned policy's actions. Our hard rules are
a domain-specific, hand-verified shield; this gives the formal framing and the vocabulary.

### 7. Action Space Reduction Strategies for Reinforcement Learning in Autonomous Driving
Elahe Delavari, Feeza Khan Khanzada, Jaerock Kwon — arXiv:2507.05251 (7 Jul 2025)
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.05251
*Why:* systematic study of how restricting the action space changes learning and safety, with a
MaskablePPO comparison. Relevant to our `legal_actions()` mask shared by all policies.

### 8. Deep Reinforcement Learning with Enhanced PPO for Safe Mobile Robot Navigation
Hamid Taheri, Seyed Rasoul Hosseini, Mohammad Ali Nekoui — arXiv:2405.16266 (25 May 2024)
https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.16266
*Why:* PPO applied to mobile-robot navigation with safety as the objective. The standard baseline
our PPO policy should be compared against in the related-work table.

### 9. Uncertainty-aware Latent Safety Filters for Avoiding Out-of-Distribution Failures
Junwon Seo, Kensuke Nakamura, Andrea Bajcsy — arXiv:2505.00779 (1 May 2025)
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.00779
*Why:* the paper closest to our WP9 diagnosis. It filters actions when the policy is outside its
training distribution — the same failure we hit on `heavy_load`. Note in the discussion that we
*tried* an uncertainty signal (feature z-scores) and rejected it as unusable, then solved the
problem by bounding the correction instead.

---

## C. Energy- and battery-aware AMR decision making (WP2/WP4/WP5)

### 10. Reinforcement Learning for AMR Charging Decisions: The Impact of Reward and Action Space Design
Janik Bischoff, Alexandru Rinciog, Anne Meyer — arXiv:2505.11136 (16 May 2025);
also LNCS *Learning and Intelligent Optimization*, DOI 10.1007/978-3-032-09156-7_20
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11136
*Why:* the single most similar paper to our decision layer. Same question — when should an AMR
charge, and how should the action space express it — and it confirms our WP5 change from one fixed
CHARGE to CHARGE 40/70/100 %.

### 11. Deep Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Battery Management of Autonomous Order Pickers
Taniya Shaji, Abhay Sobhanan, Christof Defryn — arXiv:2607.05683 (6 Jul 2026)
https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05683
*Why:* the most recent DRL-for-battery-management paper; partial vs full charging under stochastic
demand. Directly comparable to our `low_battery_start` result, where charging to 90 % first costs
21.6 units of lost production.

### 12. Fleet-Level Battery-Health-Aware Scheduling for Autonomous Mobile Robots
Jiachen Li, Shihao Li, Jian Chu, Wei Li, Dongmei Chen — arXiv:2603.22731 (24 Mar 2026)
https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.22731
*Why:* extends the objective to battery degradation, which our model does not include. Cite as the
natural multi-robot / battery-wear extension in future work.

### 13. Scheduling mobile robots in dynamic production environments considering battery management constraints
*Logistics Research* 18(1–2), 2025, pp. 46–
https://www.emerald.com/lore/article/18/1-2/46/1310572/Scheduling-mobile-robots-in-dynamic-production
*Why:* online scheduling with utility functions comparing "do the task" against "go and charge" —
structurally the same trade-off our symbolic priority tiers encode, but solved by auction instead
of by rules plus a learned ranking.

### 14. In-plant autonomous mobile robot scheduling and routing problem considering battery consumption model
Zhaofang Mao, Zhanghuang Xie, Kan Fang et al. — *Transportation Research Part C*, 2026.
DOI 10.1016/j.trc.2025.105488
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trc.2025.105488
*Why:* load-dependent battery consumption inside a factory, i.e. the optimisation-theoretic version
of our `robot_model.energy_wh`. Good for the "exact methods vs. learned policies" paragraph.

### 15. Rethinking Energy Management for Autonomous Ground Robots on a Budget
Akshar Chavan, Rudra Joshi, Marco Brocanelli — arXiv:2502.01858 (3 Feb 2025)
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.01858
*Why:* supports our most quoteable finding — that on a small robot the *computer and sensors*
dominate the energy budget, not the motors (6 of 7 Wh/h in `balanced`). Essential citation for
the WP2-revision section.

### 16. Energy-Constrained Hybrid Repair for Lifelong Multi-Agent Path Finding in Smart Warehouses
Riyang Luo, Can Lu, Jin He et al. — *Electronics* 15(12):2719, 2026. DOI 10.3390/electronics15122719
https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15122719
*Why:* lifelong operation with battery constraints and shared chargers. The multi-robot
generalisation of our single-robot shift; cite in future work.

---

## D. Energy models and their calibration — justifying `params.yaml` (WP2 revision)

### 17. Energy Utilization Prediction Techniques for Heterogeneous Mobile Robots: A Review
Krystian Góra, Grzegorz Granosik, Bartłomiej Cybulski — *Energies* 17(13):3256, 2024.
DOI 10.3390/en17133256
https://doi.org/10.3390/en17133256
*Why:* the survey that places our analytic drive + idle + payload model among the alternatives, and
gives published Wh/km ranges to defend our 9.3 Wh/km against.

### 18. A Hybrid Parameters Estimation Approach for Power Consumption Modeling of Ground Mobile Robots With Unknown Payload
Parham Haji Ali Mohamadi, Amin Khorasani, Tom Verstraten et al. — *Journal of Field Robotics*, 2025.
DOI 10.1002/rob.22470
https://doi.org/10.1002/rob.22470
*Why:* payload-dependent power for ground robots — the published counterpart of our
`payload_wh_per_m_per_kg = drive energy / robot mass`. Use it to justify that coefficient.

### 19. Cross-Validated Neural Network Optimization for Explainable Energy Prediction in Industrial Mobile Robots
Danel Rico-Melgosa, Ekaitz Zulueta, Jorge Rodriguez-Guerra et al. — *Applied Sciences* 15(23):12644, 2025.
DOI 10.3390/app152312644
https://doi.org/10.3390/app152312644
*Why:* finds angular velocity and linear acceleration to be the dominant energy predictors, with
payload secondary. That is the measured justification for WP8's turning-rate metric, and it also
explains why our planner comparison found only a ~2 % energy difference.

### 20. Energy Efficiency in Robotics Software: A Systematic Literature Review (2020–2024)
Aryan Gupta — arXiv:2508.12170 (16 Aug 2025)
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.12170
*Why:* reviews energy efficiency at the *software* level, which is where our thesis intervenes —
the decision policy, not the hardware. Good framing for the contribution statement.

---

## Runners-up (verified, use if a chapter needs more depth)

| # | Paper | Link | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | Macenski, Booker, Wallace, Fischer — *Open-Source, Cost-Aware Kinematically Feasible Planning for Mobile and Surface Robotics* (arXiv:2401.13078, Jan 2024) | https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.13078 | WP8: the Smac planner paper by the Nav2 maintainer — the primary source for the planners we benchmarked |
| R2 | Bergs, Huber, Moriz et al. — *Evaluating mobile robot navigation behavior in flexible assembly systems through digital twin and real-world experiments*, *Discover Robotics*, 2025 | https://doi.org/10.1007/s44430-025-00010-4 | WP9 tier 2: quantifying the simulator-to-reality gap, same method as our Gazebo-vs-fast-sim table |
| R3 | Borse, Viehmann, Ferrein, Lakemeyer — *A ROS 2-based Navigation and Simulation Stack for the Robotino* (arXiv:2411.09441, Nov 2024) | https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.09441 | WP1/WP3: ROS 2 + Nav2 in a logistics environment, with sim/real consistency reported |
| R4 | Salimpour, Peña-Queralta, Paez-Granados, Heikkonen, Westerlund — *Sim-to-Real Transfer for Mobile Robots with RL: from NVIDIA Isaac Sim to Gazebo and Real ROS 2 Robots* (arXiv:2501.02902, Jan 2025) | https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.02902 | WP4: why a fast surrogate simulator must be validated against the physics simulator |
| R5 | Keith & La — *Review of Autonomous Mobile Robots for the Warehouse Environment* (arXiv:2406.08333, Jun 2024) | https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.08333 | Introduction: the general AMR survey to open the related-work chapter with |
| R6 | Sotomi, Kodi, Arab — *Trust Through Transparency: Explainable Social Navigation for Autonomous Mobile Robots via Vision-Language Models* (arXiv:2504.05477, Apr 2025) | https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05477 | Explainability: measured trust gains (+16.7 %) when a robot explains itself — supports our per-decision explanation strings |

---

## Gap statement this list supports

Across all 20, none combines (a) a symbolic layer that makes safety *structural* rather than
learned, (b) a bounded neural correction on top of it, (c) a physically calibrated energy/thermal/
wear model, and (d) validation of the same policy object in a fast surrogate simulator *and* in
Gazebo with a full Nav2 stack. The battery papers (10–16) optimise scheduling without
interpretability; the neuro-symbolic papers (1–4) give interpretability without a resource model;
the safe-RL papers (5–9) give safety machinery without an industrial energy objective. That
intersection is the thesis's claim to novelty.

lines: +# Related work — 20 recent papers (2024–2026)
+Compiled 2026-09-20 for *"Towards Autonomous Industrial Mobility: An AI Framework for Optimal
+Path Planning and Resource-Efficient Navigation"*.
+Every entry was verified against the arXiv API or Crossref on the compile date: title, authors,
+year and identifier are taken from the publisher's metadata, not from memory. Each paper is
+mapped to the part of this thesis it supports.
+## A. Neuro-symbolic decision making — the core contribution (WP5/WP6/WP9)
+### 1. BANSAI: Towards Bridging the AI Adoption Gap in Industrial Robotics with Neurosymbolic Programming
+Benjamin Alt, Julia Dvorak, Darko Katic, Rainer Jäkel, Michael Beetz, Gisela Lanza — arXiv:2404.13652 (21 Apr 2024)
+https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.13652
+*Why it matters here:* the closest published statement of this thesis's premise — that industrial
+robotics adopts AI only when learned components sit inside a symbolic, inspectable program. Cite
+it in the introduction as the motivation for a hybrid rather than an end-to-end policy.
+### 2. Neuro-Symbolic Reinforcement Learning for Context-Aware Decision Making in Safe Autonomous Vehicles
+Huma Khan, Tarunika D. Chaudhari, J. V. N. Ramesh, A. Smitha Kranthi, E. Muniyandy, Y. A. B. El-Ebiary,
+D. N. P. Devadhas — IJACSA 16(5), 2025. DOI 10.14569/IJACSA.2025.0160558
+*Why:* same architecture pattern as ours — a symbolic layer enforcing hard rules, a neural layer
+ranking within what the rules allow, and an explanation for every decision. Different domain
+(driving), so it is a comparison point, not a competitor.
+### 3. Supporting Human-Robot Collaboration and Safety with the Proposed Explainable Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning
+Rafał Kozik, Aleksandra Pawlicka, Marek Pawlicki et al. — LNCS, *Availability, Reliability and Security*, 2025.
+*Why:* argues explicitly that safety in industrial robotics needs symbolic reasoning to be
+auditable. Supports our WP9 finding that only the rule-carrying policies were safe by construction.
+### 4. CausalTrace: A Neurosymbolic Causal Analysis Agent for Smart Manufacturing
+Chathurangi Shyalika, Aryaman Sharma, Fadi El Kalach et al. — arXiv:2510.12033 (14 Oct 2025)
+https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.12033
+*Why:* neurosymbolic reasoning over factory state, with interpretability as the stated goal.
+Useful for positioning our symbolic layer as part of a wider 2025 trend in manufacturing AI.
+## B. Safe learning, action masking and shielding — the PPO comparison and the ±1 bound (WP6/WP9)
+### 5. Integrating Human Knowledge Through Action Masking in Reinforcement Learning for Operations Research
+Mirko Stappert, Bernhard Lutz, Niklas Goby, Dirk Neumann — arXiv:2504.02662 (3 Apr 2025)
+https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.02662
+*Why:* the direct reference for our MaskablePPO baseline and for the `ppo_unmasked` ablation.
+It formalises masking as injecting human knowledge — exactly the question our ablation answers
+empirically (without the mask, PPO scores 28.2 and is unsafe in 11.7 % of shifts).
+### 6. Realizable Continuous-Space Shields for Safe Reinforcement Learning
+Kyungmin Kim, Davide Corsi, Andoni Rodriguez et al. — arXiv:2410.02038 (2 Oct 2024)
+https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.02038
+*Why:* shielding = a correctness layer that filters a learned policy's actions. Our hard rules are
+a domain-specific, hand-verified shield; this gives the formal framing and the vocabulary.
+### 7. Action Space Reduction Strategies for Reinforcement Learning in Autonomous Driving
+Elahe Delavari, Feeza Khan Khanzada, Jaerock Kwon — arXiv:2507.05251 (7 Jul 2025)
+https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.05251
+*Why:* systematic study of how restricting the action space changes learning and safety, with a
+MaskablePPO comparison. Relevant to our `legal_actions()` mask shared by all policies.
+### 8. Deep Reinforcement Learning with Enhanced PPO for Safe Mobile Robot Navigation
+Hamid Taheri, Seyed Rasoul Hosseini, Mohammad Ali Nekoui — arXiv:2405.16266 (25 May 2024)
+https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.16266
+*Why:* PPO applied to mobile-robot navigation with safety as the objective. The standard baseline
+our PPO policy should be compared against in the related-work table.
+### 9. Uncertainty-aware Latent Safety Filters for Avoiding Out-of-Distribution Failures
+Junwon Seo, Kensuke Nakamura, Andrea Bajcsy — arXiv:2505.00779 (1 May 2025)
+https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.00779
+*Why:* the paper closest to our WP9 diagnosis. It filters actions when the policy is outside its
+training distribution — the same failure we hit on `heavy_load`. Note in the discussion that we
+*tried* an uncertainty signal (feature z-scores) and rejected it as unusable, then solved the
+problem by bounding the correction instead.
+## C. Energy- and battery-aware AMR decision making (WP2/WP4/WP5)
+### 10. Reinforcement Learning for AMR Charging Decisions: The Impact of Reward and Action Space Design
+Janik Bischoff, Alexandru Rinciog, Anne Meyer — arXiv:2505.11136 (16 May 2025);
+also LNCS *Learning and Intelligent Optimization*, DOI 10.1007/978-3-032-09156-7_20
+https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11136
+*Why:* the single most similar paper to our decision layer. Same question — when should an AMR
+charge, and how should the action space express it — and it confirms our WP5 change from one fixed
+CHARGE to CHARGE 40/70/100 %.
+### 11. Deep Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Battery Management of Autonomous Order Pickers
+Taniya Shaji, Abhay Sobhanan, Christof Defryn — arXiv:2607.05683 (6 Jul 2026)
+https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05683
+*Why:* the most recent DRL-for-battery-management paper; partial vs full charging under stochastic
+demand. Directly comparable to our `low_battery_start` result, where charging to 90 % first costs
+21.6 units of lost production.
+### 12. Fleet-Level Battery-Health-Aware Scheduling for Autonomous Mobile Robots
+Jiachen Li, Shihao Li, Jian Chu, Wei Li, Dongmei Chen — arXiv:2603.22731 (24 Mar 2026)
+https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.22731
+*Why:* extends the objective to battery degradation, which our model does not include. Cite as the
+natural multi-robot / battery-wear extension in future work.
+### 13. Scheduling mobile robots in dynamic production environments considering battery management constraints
+*Logistics Research* 18(1–2), 2025, pp. 46–
+https://www.emerald.com/lore/article/18/1-2/46/1310572/Scheduling-mobile-robots-in-dynamic-production
+*Why:* online scheduling with utility functions comparing "do the task" against "go and charge" —
+structurally the same trade-off our symbolic priority tiers encode, but solved by auction instead
+of by rules plus a learned ranking.
+### 14. In-plant autonomous mobile robot scheduling and routing problem considering battery consumption model
+Zhaofang Mao, Zhanghuang Xie, Kan Fang et al. — *Transportation Research Part C*, 2026.
+*Why:* load-dependent battery consumption inside a factory, i.e. the optimisation-theoretic version
+of our `robot_model.energy_wh`. Good for the "exact methods vs. learned policies" paragraph.
+### 15. Rethinking Energy Management for Autonomous Ground Robots on a Budget
+Akshar Chavan, Rudra Joshi, Marco Brocanelli — arXiv:2502.01858 (3 Feb 2025)
+https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.01858
+*Why:* supports our most quoteable finding — that on a small robot the *computer and sensors*
+dominate the energy budget, not the motors (6 of 7 Wh/h in `balanced`). Essential citation for
+the WP2-revision section.
+### 16. Energy-Constrained Hybrid Repair for Lifelong Multi-Agent Path Finding in Smart Warehouses
+Riyang Luo, Can Lu, Jin He et al. — *Electronics* 15(12):2719, 2026. DOI 10.3390/electronics15122719
+https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15122719
+*Why:* lifelong operation with battery constraints and shared chargers. The multi-robot
+generalisation of our single-robot shift; cite in future work.
+## D. Energy models and their calibration — justifying `params.yaml` (WP2 revision)
+### 17. Energy Utilization Prediction Techniques for Heterogeneous Mobile Robots: A Review
+Krystian Góra, Grzegorz Granosik, Bartłomiej Cybulski — *Energies* 17(13):3256, 2024.
+*Why:* the survey that places our analytic drive + idle + payload model among the alternatives, and
+gives published Wh/km ranges to defend our 9.3 Wh/km against.
+### 18. A Hybrid Parameters Estimation Approach for Power Consumption Modeling of Ground Mobile Robots With Unknown Payload
+Parham Haji Ali Mohamadi, Amin Khorasani, Tom Verstraten et al. — *Journal of Field Robotics*, 2025.
+https://doi.org/10.1002/rob.22470
+*Why:* payload-dependent power for ground robots — the published counterpart of our
+`payload_wh_per_m_per_kg = drive energy / robot mass`. Use it to justify that coefficient.
+### 19. Cross-Validated Neural Network Optimization for Explainable Energy Prediction in Industrial Mobile Robots
+Danel Rico-Melgosa, Ekaitz Zulueta, Jorge Rodriguez-Guerra et al. — *Applied Sciences* 15(23):12644, 2025.
+*Why:* finds angular velocity and linear acceleration to be the dominant energy predictors, with
+payload secondary. That is the measured justification for WP8's turning-rate metric, and it also
+explains why our planner comparison found only a ~2 % energy difference.
+### 20. Energy Efficiency in Robotics Software: A Systematic Literature Review (2020–2024)
+Aryan Gupta — arXiv:2508.12170 (16 Aug 2025)
+https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.12170
+*Why:* reviews energy efficiency at the *software* level, which is where our thesis intervenes —
+the decision policy, not the hardware. Good framing for the contribution statement.

Based on the search results, here are the key findings related to neuro-symbolic hybrid knowledge-based reinforcement learning for robot task planning in industrial applications in 2025:

## Recent Developments

A neuro-symbolic framework called Cognition-inspired Robot Learning and Manipulation (CRLM) tightly couples structured task knowledge, semi-supervised perception, and residual reinforcement learning for efficient skill acquisition and robust execution. This framework is designed to address robotic assembly challenges in semi-structured environments for flexible manufacturing.

## Integration Approaches

Current approaches aim towards real-life robotic tasks in an Industry 4.0 setting where a digital twin is available. Research has combined symbolic planning with reinforcement learning, with approaches like PEORL integrating symbolic planning and hierarchical reinforcement learning to improve performance by achieving rapid policy search and robust symbolic planning.

## Research Areas

The search results reveal several active research directions:
- Few-shot neuro-symbolic imitation learning for long-horizon planning and acting
- Learning neuro-symbolic skills for bilevel planning

Neurosymbolic AI represents a hybrid approach that integrates neural networks' learning capabilities with symbolic AI's structured reasoning, overcoming the limitations of both paradigms. This approach leverages the strengths of both by enabling efficient knowledge extraction and conceptual reasoning, requiring less training data while maintaining transparency and adaptability in uncertain environments.

Neurorobotic approaches, which combine neural networks and robotics, offer new possibilities for AV (autonomous vehicle) decision-making and planning. *Why it matters here:* the closest peer-reviewed analogue to our architecture — a learned policy
whose symbolic part stays readable and **editable** after training. Our symbolic layer is
hand-written rather than learned, which is a difference worth defending explicitly in the
discussion. Top-tier venue; use this as the anchor citation for the neuro-symbolic claim.

### 2. Supporting Human-Robot Collaboration and Safety with the Proposed Explainable Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning
Rafał Kozik, Aleksandra Pawlicka, Marek Pawlicki et al. — **LNCS, Availability, Reliability and
Security (ARES) 2025**, book chapter. DOI 10.1007/978-3-032-00642-4_15
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-00642-4_15

inferred. Direct support for our WP9 result that only the rule-carrying policies were safe in all

### 3. Adaptive and transparent decision-making in autonomous robots through graph-structured world models
Site Hu, Takato Horii, Takayuki Nagai — **Advanced Robotics**, 2024. DOI 10.1080/01691864.2024.2415995
https://doi.org/10.1080/01691864.2024.2415995

Bettina Könighofer, Roderick Bloem, Nils Jansen, Sebastian Junges, Stefan Pranger —

https://doi.org/10.1145/3715958

### 5. Towards robust shielded reinforcement learning through adaptive constraints and exploration: the fear field framework
Haritz Odriozola-Olalde, Maider Zamalloa, Nestor Arana-Arexolaleiba, Jon Perez-Cerrolaza —
**Engineering Applications of Artificial Intelligence**, 2025. DOI 10.1016/j.engappai.2025.110055
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.engappai.2025.110055
*Why:* shielding with *adaptive* constraint strength — conceptually the nearest published relative

https://doi.org/10.3390/technologies13120573

*Why:* the same two-layer method as ours — train and decide against a fast digital model, then run

### 15. Cross-Validated Neural Network Optimization for Explainable Energy Prediction in Industrial Mobile Robots
Danel Rico-Melgosa, Ekaitz Zulueta, Jorge Rodriguez-Guerra et al. — **Applied Sciences**,

### 17. A ROS 2-Based Navigation and Simulation Stack for the Robotino
Saurabh Borse, Tarik Viehmann, Alexander Ferrein, Gerhard Lakemeyer — **LNCS, RoboCup 2024: Robot

*Why:* ROS 2 + Nav2 in a logistics environment, with simulation and real-robot runs reported side

Lukas Bergs, Meike Huber, Alexander Moriz et al. — **Discover Robotics**, 2025.

Yuexia Tang, Muhammad Aizzat Zakaria, Maryam Younas — **Sensors**, 25(4):1206, 2025.

### 20. Advancing mobile robot navigation with DRL and heuristic rewards: A comprehensive review
Mazbahur Rahman Khan, Azhar Mohd Ibrahim, Suaib Al Mahmud, Farah Asyiqin Samat, Farahiyah Jasni,

https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neucom.2025.131036
*Why:* surveys exactly the learned-vs-heuristic boundary this thesis sits on. Use it to argue that
the field's usual hybrid is "heuristics shaping the reward", whereas ours is "rules constraining
the action set" — a different and stronger guarantee.

| Paper | Link | Use for |
|---|---|---|

| Khan, Chaudhari, Ramesh et al. — *Neuro-Symbolic Reinforcement Learning for Context-Aware Decision Making in Safe Autonomous Vehicles*, **IJACSA** 16(5), 2025 | https://doi.org/10.14569/IJACSA.2025.0160558 | Architecturally very close to ours (symbolic rules + neural ranking + explanation), **but IJACSA is a weak, low-selectivity venue.** Cite only as supporting evidence, never as the anchor for the neuro-symbolic claim. |

These are all closely related and would otherwise have made the list. Each was dropped for a stated
reason, so they can be reinstated if the constraints change before submission.

| Paper | Venue | Why excluded |
|---|---|---|
| Macenski, Booker, Wallace, Fischer — *Cost-Aware Kinematically Feasible Planning for Mobile and Surface Robotics* | IEEE Robotics and Automation Practice | Peer-reviewed, but **2026** |
| Bischoff, Rinciog, Meyer — *Reinforcement Learning for AMR Charging Decisions: The Impact of Reward and Action Space Design* | LNCS (LION) | Peer-reviewed, but **2026** |
| Mao, Xie, Fang — *In-plant autonomous mobile robot scheduling and routing problem considering battery consumption model* | Transportation Research Part C | Peer-reviewed, but **2026** |
| Luo, Lu, He — *Energy-Constrained Hybrid Repair for Lifelong Multi-Agent Path Finding in Smart Warehouses* | Electronics | Peer-reviewed, but **2026** |
| Zhang, Yan, Hu — *Deep reinforcement learning for dynamic scheduling of energy-efficient automated guided vehicles* | Journal of Intelligent Manufacturing | Peer-reviewed, but **2023** |
| Alt, Dvorak, Katic et al. — *BANSAI: Bridging the AI Adoption Gap in Industrial Robotics with Neurosymbolic Programming* | — | **arXiv preprint only** |
| Stappert, Lutz, Goby, Neumann — *Integrating Human Knowledge Through Action Masking in RL for Operations Research* | — | **arXiv preprint only** |
| Seo, Nakamura, Bajcsy — *Uncertainty-aware Latent Safety Filters for Avoiding Out-of-Distribution Failures* | — | **arXiv preprint only** |
| Chavan, Joshi, Brocanelli — *Rethinking Energy Management for Autonomous Ground Robots on a Budget* | — | **arXiv preprint only** |
| Keith & La — *Review of Autonomous Mobile Robots for the Warehouse Environment* | — | **arXiv preprint only** |

Two of these hurt more than the others, and the gap should be acknowledged in the text rather than
hidden: **Macenski et al.** is the primary source for the Smac planners benchmarked in WP8 (its
Nav2 documentation can be cited instead), and **Chavan et al.** is the closest published support for
our finding that electronics idle power dominates a small robot's energy budget (6 of 7 Wh/h in
`balanced`) — for that claim, reference 14 (Energies 2024) is the peer-reviewed substitute.

---

## Gap statement this list supports

None of the 20 combines all four of: (a) a symbolic layer making safety **structural** rather than
learned, (b) a **bounded** neural correction on top of it, (c) a physically calibrated
energy/thermal/wear model, and (d) validation of the **same policy object** in a fast surrogate
simulator *and* in Gazebo with a full Nav2 stack.

The scheduling papers (8–13) optimise energy and throughput without interpretability or a safety
guarantee; the neuro-symbolic papers (1–3) give interpretability without an industrial resource
model; the safe-RL papers (4–7) give the safety machinery without an energy objective or a real
navigation stack; the energy papers (14–16) model consumption without deciding anything. That
intersection is the thesis's claim to novelty.
